items.title: Building Legal Agents When You Can't See the Data - Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora
items.content: Legora can’t read a single trace of what its agent does for a lawyer. The data belongs to the law firm’s clients. How do you build and test an agent when you can’t see its work? Jacob Lauritzen is the CTO of Legora, one of the fastest-growing companies in legal tech history. The team started in a Stockholm basement with ChatGPT, Swedish law, and a search tool. Today, a lawyer can use Legora to draft and edit Word documents, review 10,000 contracts in a single table, or run due diligence. The agent also coordinates work between lawyers, clients, and other agents. When Legora made its own acquisitions, the team used it for diligence. What we talked about • Why Legora resisted adding a model picker for years, and why it finally added one • Jacob’s estimate that models already do about 60% of legal work well, and why the rest takes a smarter model • How three engineers and three lawyers build test environments modeled on customers’ work, much like the “worlds” used in reinforcement learning • A citation problem where the model got it right 70% of the time, then 99% after one release. Legora didn’t have to change anything. • Why Legora runs everything on Azure and why it doesn’t use ElevenLabs • Tabular Review, the million-cell spreadsheet the industry copied down to the name • How intake works, how agents create lists, and how a list can start another agent • What legal engineers and forward-deployed engineers each do, and who gets to write code • The 300 Spartans slide Jacob used to argue that 20 engineers would be enough forever. Now there are 100, and he still feels short-handed. • Why Jacob finds Fable and Opus too chatty for drafting and likes Astra’s concise writing • Why drafting a long contract is a search problem • Whether model labs will cut off legal tools the way they cut off coding tools • What happens to law firm partnerships, the billable hour, and jobs for junior lawyers Legora is hiring engineers in New York, Stockholm, and London. items.title: Korea’s Stock Market Crashed $1 Trillion. What Does That Mean for the Global AI Race?
items.content: Richard Gray is an analyst who works for a foreign policy think tank in Washington, D.C. Since 2025, South Korea’s capital markets have vacillated from the world’s best-performing to shedding more than $1 trillion in market capitalization. This volatility is a story of how Korea’s financial system overlays supply chain specialization. With Korean firms Samsung and SK hynix controlling a majority share of global memory, South Korea’s stock market functionally operates as a single, highly leveraged node within the AI financial architecture. Two interwoven dynamics explain the convulsions of Korean capital markets and their global ramifications. The first is the Korea discount , in which Korean equities are structurally undervalued because of lagging financial development and weak corporate governance. The second is a memory discount , with each leading high-bandwidth memory (HBM) company (Micron in the U.S., SK hynix and Samsung in Korea) having depressed valuations in their respective markets. The June-July 2026 crash rippled far beyond Korea’s borders and forewarns what may be to come in future market corrections. For Korea, its historically shallow capital markets and exposure to the memory sector — which is now facing emergent Chinese competitors — serve as overlapping pressures on its financial position. In this environment, the threat of a market correction cascading across global markets and the U.S.-China tech competition looms large. The Zenith: Capital Infusion The Korean market is essentially a bet on two companies competing in the same industry. Korea’s memory chip industry has driven exponential year-on-year growth in Korea’s capital markets. From March 2025 to June 2026, the KOSPI — Korea’s main stock index — rose 241%, adding nearly $3.3 trillion in capitalization and exceeding the total increase accumulated over the index’s 43-year history (Bloomberg). items.title: Is Half of China’s AI Making Slop?
items.content: Zilan Qian is a research scholar at GovAI researching AI development and regulation in China. On October 21, the People’s Daily published a commentary titled “Turning ‘Gunpowder’ into ‘Fireworks’? Beware the Claim That China’s AI Has Gone Astray” (把”火药”做成”烟花”？警惕”中国AI跑偏论”). The same day, Nanfang Commentary (南方评论), the op-ed column of Southern Daily , asked : “Is Half of China’s Compute Being Spent on Feel-Good Dramas (爽剧)? Don’t Judge AI by Its Tokens.” Three days earlier, Beijing News (新京报) had questioned whether “‘American AI Boosts Productivity While Chinese AI Makes Tittytainment’ Is a False Proposition.” All three state-affiliated outlets were responding to the same viral claim: that 55% of China’s AI tokens were being used for short dramas and video generation. The claim struck a nerve because AI-generated entertainment in China is both everywhere and widely despised. According to China’s broadcasting regulator, more than 90% of the roughly 430,000 micro-dramas released in the first eight months of 2026 were AI productions. Yet Chinese media and public figures routinely call them wunao (无脑, braindead), cuzhi lanzao (粗制滥造, shoddily made), and zhili dixia (智力低下, intellectually deficient). 1 Why, in a society that places such a premium on productivity, has an industry devoted to manufacturing seemingly useless pleasure become so enormously popular? And what should we make of the shame attached to it? I argue that both answers lie in Chinese society’s obsession with usefulness, where technologies and people alike are judged by their productive value, so much so that resting can feel…

items.title: Xi vs Trump on Corruption
items.content: In February, Eric and Donald Jr. sat down with a reporter to explain why Abu Dhabi paid $500m for a stake in World Liberty Financial. Don Jr. said, “They tried all this nonsense the first time around. Frankly, it’s gotten old…They created this monster.” The monster of political corruption has been with us since the founding. But since the Progressive Eva, it has been cut with at least a tinge of embarrassment. The Trumps instead have done it in broad daylight and tried to make it a flex. China’s political system is riddled with corruption on an entirely different scale. The skims in China happen up and down the system, and making a billion dollars while in office is nothing new for senior Chinese leaders. But Xi understands what this costs the Party. In his first Politburo speech as General Secretary, he warned that corruption, left to spread, would “doom the Party and the state.” Xi was horrified by seeing youth with bloodlines just as red as his crash foreign sports cars in the streets of Beijing. He views the princeling inheritance as a responsibility to serve, not a license to fuckboy. As Kamil Galeev writes , Xi aims to extirpate “the alien, unfamiliar, threatening bandit entrepreneurial culture — not even from the country but rather, from the national elites.” Xi is a believer, but Trump is a businessman. After Trump brought down the guardrails with a compliant SCOTUS and Congress, the presidential family has been sloppily revenue-maximizing ever since. 1 Xi’s anti-corruption campaign hasn’t liquidated corruption in China, which still lubricates a much higher percentage of economic activity than similar behavior does in America. But Xi has succeeded in making it dangerous. Making outside money in Xi’s China runs the risk of execution — far different stakes than embarrassing ProPublica articles revealing crimes that get pardoned away. Make corruption cringe again! To maintain leadership and establish the next world order, the U.S. is moving to cement its lead. Barnett Koven is a Managing Director of AI and Data at Accenture Federal Services . He came to Accenture Federal Services after stints in industry and a faculty job at the University of Maryland, where his counterinsurgency research showed that some of the most influential quantitative studies got the answer exactly backwards. We discuss… Why “inaction is in and of itself risky” — and how government risk-aversion compounds against less-cautious competitors The “gun-armor race” in classified AI environments, where defense costs grow exponentially against linear offense Entity resolution and predictive modeling for BIS export-control enforcement, and unwrapping the PLA’s shell-company maze DOE’s Genesis Mission and Accenture Federal’s “backbone for scientific research” Thank you to Accenture Federal Services for bringing us this episode. Listen now on your favorite podcast app . From COIN to Genesis Jordan Schneider: Let’s do a bit of the career arc. How do we get from a PhD on COIN to DOE and the Genesis mission? Barnett Koven: Absolutely. I spent a lot of time in Latin America and saw the aftereffects of some virulent insurgencies in Peru and Colombia in particular, ended up doing a PhD studying the spatiotemporal diffusion of insurgent violence as a result of counterinsurgency strategy — specifically as a result of development assistance and other non-kinetic interventions during counterinsurgency. Really loved that, and sought out the opportunity to do more policy-relevant research, which is not necessarily the norm at the academy. items.content: As an engineer-focused newsletter we only very rarely let financial stories through (our last example was Jan 2025 ), but when this is about the future of Google and Google Search , with a recently departed AI leadership, you cannot not care. At its heart is the tension between overview pages and underlying pages they summarize. Any good enough summary obviates the need for you reading the source. Google’s Featured Snippets or Knowledge Panels have long had that tension with the publishers that supply that data. But now, Google’s own AI Overviews are potentially affecting traffic with… Google's Search revenue. Google doesn’t break out AI Mode in sufficient detail that we can make any sort of rigorous analysis, but most people are quoting Philipp Schindler (Chief Business Officer): “It’s worth noting that the strong growth in AI Mode queries had an impact because of the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode.” Together with other bad earnings results it set off a range of steep declines throughout tech: View post on X ↗ This is against a backdrop of souring tech/AI sentiment in public markets - and with OpenAI raising at $1.25T not $1.4T , not the sort of thing you want in the lead up to one of the biggest tech IPOs of all time. items.content: People were asking us about Mythos and everything, even though I think realistically a lot of legal work does not require Mythos-level intelligence. Paralegals, gone. Yeah. It's just like we did nothing and, like, great. But if you're doing a, you know, four hundred million dollar M&A transaction, you're gonna want Lagora. We're just gonna be twenty engineers for the rest of the company's history, and, like, we're gonna beat everyone who's much bigger. Uh, we're a hundred engineers now, and it feels like we're way too small. But it's something that I'm toying with is, like, how much of our product can just be the agent versus all the other stuff? [upbeat music] Okay, we're here in the studio with special guest, uh, Jacob Lauridsen, CTO of Lagora. Did I get it right, Lauridsen? Lauridsen. That's fine. Yeah, that's okay. And that's Danish. I'm not super sure that how... It's Danish, yeah, exactly. Does it have a special history behind it? It's just, no, sen is like son, son of. Son of Laurits. So just like you have son and... Yeah. [laughs] So son of Laurits, that's my name. [laughs] Nice. Uh, we've crossed paths here and there. You, you, you spoke at, uh, AI a few times, and obviously Lagora is one of the fastest-growing legal tech in history. Yep. And, uh, y- you said something at the start in our pre-show that I thought was really interesting. You said that your origin is very European. Mm-hmm. Uh, even though obviously you're expanding in New York and SF, what feels different about your culture? I think we are just at the core probably very, uh, humble about what we're doing because we've always been the underdog from the very beginning. No one believed the smallest startup in a basement in Stockholm was gonna, you know, out-compete this huge behemoth that was, like, way, yeah, ahead of us in the US. So I think we've always been underdogs, and so we've always been very humble. Um, we've always sort of had to fight for our, uh, existence. Um, I think something we've had to learn as we've also become more and more, um... as we've entered the US and been in the US a lot more, is to be a little bit more, uh, bold and, like, s-s-tell the world how great we are 'cause it, it doesn't come naturally to, I think, some of us. I kinda wanna start by going over your guys' product, 'cause I feel like with a lot of these, like, legal products, you know, they're kinda, like, under wraps. Like, you know- Yeah, sure. [laughs]... you're not supposed to, like, show it. But, um, yeah, if you could just talk about, like, what does the product look like and maybe, like, how did you guys get there? Like, like, what have been the product iterations that got you- Hmm... to where you are today? I think that would be really interesting. Yeah, absolutely. The way everything started was ChatGPT with, uh, Swedish laws- Okay... and search tool in it. That was literally the entire everything. And so that's where we started. We started with legal research, which is, like, a huge market basically in the world where, um, lawyers spend a lot of time figuring out what are previous cases that look like this? What's the legal precedent? Like, is this... You know, what have previous people done in these situations? That's extremely important. Um, and so that has always been part of our product. Basically, we started from, like, an, an agent you could ask questions, then it would query laws. That was the very simple beginning. Um, and then from that, it's expanded, and so it's expanded in, like, what can the agent do? It, it will now, uh, you know, draft a lot of stuff really well. It will edit Word files. items.title: How Anthropic ships Claude with Claude: Separating the Brain from the Hands
items.content: Watch the full episode on YouTube As we learned from the Anthropic S-1 filings yesterday , the lab has some of the highest revenue and research efficiency in human history, particularly with -126% loss to 19% GAAP profit turnaround in the last year. The company credits this to their two core loops: Improvement and Investment: Today we go inside how Anthropic works. Now the dust has settled on Opus 5.5 and it has lasted a month as the generally accepted #1 LLM in the world, we dive into its launch, and how Anthropic ships Claude with Claude with Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang , heads of Engineering and Product respectively. The team is working under two kinds of pressure. The models are getting more capable, which makes safe deployment and access decisions harder. At the same time, usage is growing fast enough that ordinary infrastructure choices—like how much CPU an API consumes—become strategic. Those problems meet in the product choices that reach developers. A model launch is also an API launch Anthropic's Opus 5.5 launch emphasizes both model quality and cost. We discuss feedback that the previous Opus generations were be too verbose, alongside the need for stronger intelligence per dollar. Anthropic says the new model costs less to run than its predecessor; the exact saving depends on the workload and its use of cached context. The less visible launch work involves changes to how people integrate the API. One example we discuss is protecting model reasoning against extraction used for distillation. Preserving thinking blocks across turns helps address this, but a new requirement can also break a customer's existing harness. Katelyn also describes what being part of early access programs actually looks like in practice: Customers run evaluations in their own harnesses, report surprising behavior, and sometimes pass along less formal impressions. The useful part is not just a benchmark score: it is seeing the model in environments and tasks Anthropic's own produ…

items.title: Can You Use AI To Make Good Art? — With Fred Graver
items.content: Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:18 The industry is in a tailspin. There are fewer opportunities for writers and producers and people who make things. And I really had the conviction that AI can help you figure out who you are, how you have to survive in this world, and also how to make things that will then promote you and promote your career. Speaker 2 | 00:18 - 00:40 Depending on who you ask, right now is an apocalypse for creative people, or it's like the best time to be alive ever. I think it's it's one of the most important questions about AI as a technology. Can you use it to make good art, or can you only use it to make slop? That's why I'm extremely excited for this episode. My cohost Natalia Quintero interviewed Fred Graver. Speaker 2 | 00:40 - 01:03 Fred is a four time Emmy award winning filmmaker and technologist who is using AI all the time to make really great stuff in film. And he came on to share how he uses it, how it can be used as a creative tool, and the dirty secret in Hollywood that a lot of people use it even if they won't admit to it. So Natalia, tell us about the conversation. Speaker 3 | 01:04 - 01:20 It was so cool to talk to Fred and to learn from someone who's been a leader at the top of their industry for so many decades. And what's interesting is that Fred has actually done this a few times. He started his career as a Disney Imagineer. Speaker 2 | 01:20 - 01:21 That's the coolest thing. Speaker 3 | 01:21 - 02:02 Kind of the dream jobs. And then he, you know, built this incredible career at VH1 and MTV, and then he kind of threw it all away and became the head of TV at Twitter when it was a startup, and that didn't totally make sense. But he he had this really interesting thesis of wanting to get closer and closer to the audience, And now he's done it again. You know, he's basically built what will be compound producing and rebuilt the production process from the ground up using his decades of expertise, the... Speaker 2 | 02:06 - 02:09 I love it. It's a great episode. Let's dive in. Speaker 3 | 02:21 - 02:37 So, Fred, thank you so much for being with us. And I wanna start by actually just maybe getting a little bit of background on your career and how you got here. This... Maybe let's start, at the top. You're a professional writer. Speaker 3 | 02:37 - 02:39 Yes. How did you get into that? Speaker 1 | 02:39 - 03:04 I came to New York, and, I could type over a 100 words a minute. And we are back in the day of of IBM Selectrics and printers copies and all of that. And I went to work, and, oh, and I knew how to copy edit. And I went to work at the National Lampoon. And I was hired there, because I could I could type and I could copy edit, and I wouldn't screw up the joke. Speaker 1 | 03:04 - 03:18 So a bad copy editor would go, well, this isn't grammatically correct, and I would understand, no. That's the joke. And, I began editing, stuff at the National Lampoon and writing for the National Lampoon. So that's... Yes. Speaker 1 | 03:18 - 03:45 That's how I got started, which which for for people who are watching, who are every... In the every audience, yes, your your technical skills count. They will often get you in the door, particularly to jump ahead. You know, the whole kind of you're gonna get replaced by somebody who knows how to use AI. People who understand what's happening under the hood, are going to be incredibly in demand, I think. Speaker 1 | 03:45 - 04:09 So, I went to work from there for for David Letterman, for Late Night with David Letterman, and stayed there for a long time. It was a great gig. And then went to work for Norman Lear. In the seventies, Norman was the king of television. I think he had four or five hit shows in the top 10 of the Nielsen rankings at one time. To enable large-scale joint RL across hundreds of downstream domains , we optimized every layer of the stack — the RL framework, long-context inference, training efficiency, sandbox infrastructure, rollout scheduling, and a shared platform for environment quality checks — so that each increment of RL compute delivers stable, predictable returns. As a result, K3.1 Pro achieves consistent gains in every domain. AI News for 10/22/2026-10/23/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords.
